sets.title: Nomenclature worksheet · 1–20: name and type
sets.description: Work through the original 20 formulas. Choose both the compound name and ionic or covalent type. Each answer is checked separately; use Type answers whenever you want to practice recall.

rows.explanation: 1. Find the pieces: Ba is barium, a group-2 metal. Recognize CO₃ as carbonate, a whole polyatomic ion. Look up that group rather than treating its C and O as separate pieces. | 2. Decide the type: Ba²⁺ and CO₃²⁻ are oppositely charged ions, so classify the compound as ionic. The C–O bonds inside carbonate are covalent, but the compound is held together between positive and negative ions. | 3. Build the answer: Barium is Ba2+ and carbonate is the whole CO3 2− ion. Their charges balance in a 1:1 ratio. Keep carbonate intact; the compound is ionic even though carbonate contains covalent bonds. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Carbonate is not carbide: carbide has no oxygen. Carbonite is not the carbonate name in this course. Barium has the usual +2 charge, so barium(III) does not fit.

1. Find the pieces: K is potassium, a group-1 metal; Cl is chlorine, a nonmetal. In this salt the pieces are K⁺ and Cl⁻, not neutral KCl molecules. | 2. Decide the type: The oppositely charged ions make this ionic. Group 1 helps you find potassium’s +1 charge; chloride supplies −1. | 3. Build the answer: Potassium forms K+ and chloride is Cl−. A 1:1 ratio balances charge. Name the metal first, then chloride; no molecular prefix or Roman numeral is needed for this fixed-charge metal. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Chloride has no oxygen; chlorate is ClO₃⁻. The 1:1 ratio needs neither di- nor a Roman numeral for potassium.

1. Find the pieces: Pb is the metal lead and Cl is the nonmetal chlorine. In this example, treat each chlorine as a chloride ion, Cl⁻. Lead can have more than one charge. | 2. Decide the type: This is ionic: lead cations balance chloride anions. The formula contains two Cl⁻ ions, so one Pb ion must be +2 for a neutral total. | 3. Build the answer: Two chloride ions contribute −2 in total, so the one lead ion is +2. The Roman numeral II specifies that charge, not the number of chloride ions. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Lead(IV) would require four Cl⁻ ions per lead. Lead(I) would require one. Roman numerals identify the metal charge; do not use the molecular prefix di- to name this salt.

1. Find the pieces: S is sulfur and F is fluorine: both are nonmetals. SF₄ is one of this worksheet’s molecular examples; do not try to assign S⁴⁺ and four F⁻ ions just from its subscripts. | 2. Decide the type: Classify SF₄ as covalent. Its atoms are bonded by shared electron pairs, and the formula tells us one sulfur atom and four fluorine atoms. | 3. Build the answer: This is a molecular covalent compound. Four fluorine atoms give tetrafluoride; the first element is sulfur, with no mono- prefix for one atom. Prefixes count atoms rather than ionic charges. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Tetra- means four, so difluoride would give only two F atoms. Tetrasulfur would put four atoms on the wrong element. The missing prefix on sulfur means one, not zero.

1. Find the pieces: Fe is the metal iron; S is sulfur. Here sulfur is the monatomic sulfide ion, S²⁻. This is not the oxygen-containing sulfate group, SO₄²⁻. | 2. Decide the type: Iron and sulfide are the cation and anion, so this example is ionic. One Fe must supply +2 to balance one S²⁻. | 3. Build the answer: Sulfide is S2−. A single iron ion must supply +2, so the name is iron(II) sulfide. Sulfide and sulfate are different ions; sulfate contains oxygen. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Iron(III) would not balance this 1:1 sulfide formula. Sulfate would require oxygen, which FeS does not contain. The ending -ide tells you which anion is meant, but does not by itself prove ionic bonding.

1. Find the pieces: N is nitrogen and S is sulfur; both are nonmetals. Read N₂S₃ as the supplied binary covalent formula, with two N atoms and three S atoms. | 2. Decide the type: Use the covalent naming route: count the atoms named by prefixes. There is no metal cation whose charge needs a Roman numeral here. | 3. Build the answer: For this binary covalent formula, di- counts two nitrogen atoms and tri- counts three sulfur atoms. Change the second element ending to -ide: trisulfide. Do not reduce the atom counts. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Tri- belongs to sulfur and di- belongs to nitrogen. Trinitrogen disulfide reverses those counts. Sulfate contains oxygen, which this formula has none of.

1. Find the pieces: Ca is calcium, a group-2 metal. The parentheses show repeated OH groups; OH⁻ is the hydroxide ion. Keep each O and H together. | 2. Decide the type: Ca²⁺ balances two OH⁻ ions, making this ionic. Covalent bonds inside OH⁻ do not change the classification of the whole calcium hydroxide compound. | 3. Build the answer: Calcium is Ca2+ and each hydroxide group is OH−. Two intact hydroxide ions balance one calcium ion. The parentheses multiply the whole OH group; ionic naming does not use dihydroxide here. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Oxide is O²⁻ and lacks hydrogen. The 2 outside the parentheses multiplies the entire OH group. It does not mean the ionic name must contain dihydroxide.

1. Find the pieces: Co is cobalt, a metal, while F is fluorine. Notice the lowercase o: Co is one element; CO would be carbon and oxygen. | 2. Decide the type: This compound is ionic in the course model. Three F⁻ ions contribute −3, so the single cobalt ion must be Co³⁺. | 3. Build the answer: Three fluoride ions contribute −3, so cobalt must be +3. Use cobalt(III) fluoride for this ionic compound. Co is cobalt; CO would mean carbon and oxygen. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: The Roman numeral must be III. Cobalt(II) would pair with two fluorides instead. Trifluoride counts atoms, but this worksheet uses a Roman numeral to specify a variable-charge metal in an ionic salt.

1. Find the pieces: Ag is silver, a metal; Br is bromine, a nonmetal. Use the usual course ions Ag⁺ and Br⁻. | 2. Decide the type: Opposite silver and bromide ions balance 1:1, so the compound is ionic. You do not need to see written + and − signs in a neutral salt formula for ions to be present. | 3. Build the answer: The usual course ion for silver is Ag+; bromide is Br−. Their 1:1 combination is silver bromide. Bromate would contain oxygen and is a different ion. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Bromate is BrO₃⁻, so it would add oxygen. Silver(II) and dibromide do not fit the usual +1 silver ion and the printed 1:1 formula.

1. Find the pieces: K is a group-1 metal. SO₄ is the sulfate group: one S and four O atoms belong to each SO₄²⁻ ion. | 2. Decide the type: Two K⁺ ions balance one SO₄²⁻ ion, so classify the whole compound as ionic. More than two different elements does not make a compound covalent. | 3. Build the answer: Sulfate is SO4 2−. Two K+ ions balance one sulfate ion. Retain the polyatomic name sulfate and do not add a molecular prefix to potassium. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Sulfite is SO₃²⁻; sulfide is S²⁻. Neither preserves the four oxygens of sulfate. The ionic name does not use dipotassium just because two potassium ions are needed.

1. Find the pieces: Na is sodium, a group-1 metal. OH is the hydroxide group, OH⁻; it is not an oxide plus a separate hydrogen atom in this naming task. | 2. Decide the type: Na⁺ and OH⁻ balance 1:1. The compound is ionic even though the bond within the hydroxide ion is covalent. | 3. Build the answer: Na+ balances one OH− ion. OH− is hydroxide, so the ionic compound is sodium hydroxide. The hydrogen belongs to that whole polyatomic ion. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Sodium oxide would use O²⁻ without hydrogen. Hydroxide is a name worth recognizing as a whole unit. Sodium’s usual +1 charge does not call for sodium(II).

1. Find the pieces: Fe is iron, a variable-charge metal; O is oxygen. For this oxide example, each oxide ion is O²⁻. | 2. Decide the type: The compound is ionic. Three oxide ions total −6; two iron ions must total +6, so each is Fe³⁺. | 3. Build the answer: Three oxide ions contribute −6. Two iron ions share +6, making each Fe3+. The Roman numeral is III, not II from the iron subscript. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Use III for the charge on each iron. The subscript 2 counts iron ions and does not mean iron(II). Diiron trioxide follows atom-count naming, while this task uses the ionic Stock name.

1. Find the pieces: Mn is manganese, a metal. SO₄ is sulfate, SO₄²⁻. Be careful: Mn is not Mg, the symbol for magnesium. | 2. Decide the type: Manganese cations and sulfate anions make this ionic. One sulfate contributes −2, so one manganese must be +2 here. | 3. Build the answer: One sulfate ion has charge −2, so Mn must be +2 here: manganese(II) sulfate. Mn is manganese; Mg is magnesium. The sulfate subscript 4 counts oxygen atoms and is not the metal charge. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: The 4 counts oxygen atoms inside sulfate; it does not make manganese(IV). Sulfite has only three oxygens, and magnesium is a different element.

1. Find the pieces: Fe is iron and Cl is chlorine. In this salt each Cl is a chloride ion, Cl⁻. | 2. Decide the type: Metal cations and chloride anions make this ionic. Two chlorides contribute −2, so one iron must be Fe²⁺. | 3. Build the answer: Two Cl− ions balance Fe2+. The name iron(II) chloride specifies the iron charge. Molecular prefixes such as di- are not used for this ionic salt. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Iron(III) would need three chloride ions. The name’s Roman numeral gives iron’s charge. Dichloride is not the ionic naming route used for this exercise.

1. Find the pieces: This is the important no-metal case: recognize NH₄⁺ as ammonium and NO₃⁻ as nitrate. They are two whole polyatomic ions, even though every element present is a nonmetal. | 2. Decide the type: Ammonium is positive and nitrate is negative. Attraction between those ions makes the compound ionic. Bonds within each ion are covalent; the question asks about the compound as a whole. | 3. Build the answer: NH4+ is ammonium and NO3− is nitrate. These oppositely charged polyatomic ions form an ionic compound even though no metal appears. Bonds within each ion are covalent; the requested type describes the compound. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Do not choose covalent only because no metal appears. Ammonia is neutral NH₃, not NH₄⁺. Nitrite is NO₂⁻, not the nitrate group printed here.

1. Find the pieces: Mg is magnesium, a group-2 metal; O is oxygen. The usual ions for this example are Mg²⁺ and oxide, O²⁻. | 2. Decide the type: Oppositely charged ions make this ionic. Equal +2 and −2 charges balance in a 1:1 ratio; no written subscript is needed for one of each. | 3. Build the answer: Mg2+ and O2− balance in the smallest 1:1 ratio. The ionic name is magnesium oxide. Peroxide is O2 2−, a different ion; mono- is not needed here. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Oxide and peroxide are different ions: peroxide is O₂²⁻. Molecular prefixes such as mono- are not needed to name this ionic compound.

1. Find the pieces: P and O are both nonmetals. For this worksheet, follow the covalent naming route for the printed P₂O₅ formula. | 2. Decide the type: Covalent naming uses the atom counts shown: two phosphorus atoms and five oxygen atoms. Do not invent a monatomic P⁵⁺ ion from an oxidation-state calculation. | 3. Build the answer: Name the formula as printed: di- for two phosphorus atoms and pentoxide for five oxygens. Pentaoxide is also accepted. P2O5 is the conventional empirical representation of phosphorus(V) oxide; common molecular forms use P4O10. This task names the supplied formula and does not silently replace it. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Di- belongs to phosphorus and pent-oxide to oxygen. This printed P₂O₅ is the conventional empirical representation; common molecular forms use P₄O₁₀. Name what is printed here rather than silently replacing the formula.

1. Find the pieces: Cu is copper, a variable-charge metal. S is sulfide, S²⁻, in this salt. | 2. Decide the type: This is ionic. One sulfide contributes −2; the two copper ions together must contribute +2, making each Cu⁺. | 3. Build the answer: Sulfide contributes −2. Two copper ions must each contribute +1, so the correct Roman numeral is I. The subscript 2 is the copper count, not its charge. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: The Roman numeral is I. The subscript 2 counts copper ions, not their charge. Copper(II) sulfide would use CuS, and sulfate would require oxygen.

1. Find the pieces: B is boron, a metalloid; Cl is chlorine, a nonmetal. BCl₃ is a known molecular covalent example. Being left of chlorine on the periodic table is not enough to call boron a metal cation. | 2. Decide the type: Use the covalent route: one B atom and three Cl atoms are joined by shared-electron bonds. Boron halides are a useful boundary of the simple metal/nonmetal shortcut. | 3. Build the answer: Boron trichloride is a molecular covalent compound: one boron and three chlorine atoms. Boron is a metalloid, so a metal/nonmetal shortcut alone is not enough; use this known molecular example and its prefixes. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Tri- means three chlorines. Dichloride would mean two, and triboron would put three atoms on the wrong element. Do not infer ionic bonding merely because a formula is neutral.

1. Find the pieces: Zn is zinc, a metal using the usual +2 course charge. PO₄ is phosphate, a whole PO₄³⁻ ion. | 2. Decide the type: Three Zn²⁺ ions total +6, and two phosphate ions total −6. These cations and anions make the compound ionic; parentheses preserve repeated polyatomic groups. | 3. Build the answer: Three Zn2+ ions give +6 and two PO4 3− ions give −6. Name the whole phosphate ion. Zinc uses the usual +2 course charge, so the subscript 3 is not a Roman numeral III. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: The subscript 3 counts zinc ions, not a zinc(III) charge. Phosphide is P³⁻ without oxygen; phosphite has a different oxygen count from phosphate.

sets.title: Nomenclature worksheet · 21–30: formulas
sets.description: Translate each of the original 10 names into a formula. Ionic compounds use balanced whole-ion ratios; molecular prefixes specify atom counts. Choose answers first, or switch to typing.

rows.explanation: 1. Find the pieces: Nickel is a metal; the Roman numeral (II) explicitly gives Ni²⁺. Sulfide is S²⁻. Identify those two ions before deciding subscripts. | 2. Decide the type: Use the ionic route. One +2 nickel ion balances one −2 sulfide ion, so the smallest whole-ion ratio is 1:1. | 3. Build the answer: Nickel(II) is Ni2+ and sulfide is S2−. The smallest neutral ratio is 1:1: NiS. Roman numeral II sets the ion charge; it does not become a subscript automatically. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Do not copy the Roman numeral into Ni₂S: that would leave net +2. NiS₂ would leave net −2. Sulfide contains no oxygen, unlike sulfate.

1. Find the pieces: Lithium is a group-1 metal, so use Li⁺. Hydroxide means the whole OH⁻ ion. | 2. Decide the type: This is ionic: one positive lithium ion balances one negative hydroxide ion. Keep O and H together while balancing. | 3. Build the answer: Li+ and OH− combine 1:1. Keep hydroxide as OH; with only one hydroxide group, LiOH needs no parentheses. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Li₂OH would total +1; Li(OH)₂ would total −1. LiO leaves out hydrogen and substitutes oxide for hydroxide. One OH group needs no parentheses.

1. Find the pieces: Nitrogen and bromine are both nonmetals. The name already tells you to use the molecular prefix tri-, which counts atoms. | 2. Decide the type: Use the covalent route. No prefix on nitrogen means one N atom; tribromide means three Br atoms. Do not cross ion charges to find these numbers. | 3. Build the answer: The first element has one atom when no prefix is written; tri- means three bromine atoms. The molecular formula is NBr3. Element-symbol capitals matter. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: N₃Br reverses which element gets three atoms. NBr loses the tri- information. N₂Br₃ invents a di- prefix that the name does not contain.

1. Find the pieces: Ammonium is the positive polyatomic ion NH₄⁺, not neutral ammonia NH₃. Sulfide is S²⁻. No metal is needed because ammonium supplies the cation. | 2. Decide the type: Use the ionic route. Two +1 ammonium ions balance one −2 sulfide ion. The whole ammonium group must be copied twice. | 3. Build the answer: Ammonium is NH4+ and sulfide is S2−. Use two intact ammonium ions for one sulfide ion: (NH4)2S. Parentheses multiply all four hydrogens as well as nitrogen. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: NH₄S supplies only +1 against −2. The 2 belongs outside (NH₄), so it multiplies both N and all four H atoms. N₂H₄S fails to copy the complete ion twice.

1. Find the pieces: Magnesium is Mg²⁺, a group-2 metal ion. Sulfide is the monatomic S²⁻ ion. | 2. Decide the type: Use the ionic route. One magnesium ion and one sulfide ion cancel to zero, so use the simplest 1:1 whole-ion ratio. | 3. Build the answer: Mg2+ balances S2− in a 1:1 ratio: MgS. Reduce the whole-ion ratio rather than writing Mg2S2. Sulfide contains no oxygen. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Do not keep 2 and 2 as subscripts after crossing charges: Mg₂S₂ reduces to MgS for this ionic formula. Sulfate would include oxygen and answer a different question.

1. Find the pieces: Potassium is K⁺, a group-1 metal ion. Sulfate is SO₄²⁻; its four oxygens are part of each ion. | 2. Decide the type: Use the ionic route. Two potassium ions give +2, balancing one sulfate ion with −2. Change only the number of whole ions. | 3. Build the answer: Two K+ ions balance SO4 2−. The formula is K2SO4. Do not change the internal SO4 formula while balancing the ions. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: KSO₄ would still total −1. K₂SO₃ changes sulfate into sulfite. Do not change an ion’s internal subscripts while trying to balance charge.

1. Find the pieces: Nitrogen and oxygen are nonmetals. Di- and tetr(a)- are atom-count clues in this molecular name. | 2. Decide the type: Use the covalent route. Dinitrogen gives two N atoms and tetroxide gives four O atoms. These are actual molecular counts, not charges to balance. | 3. Build the answer: Di- means two nitrogen atoms and tetr(a)-oxide means four oxygens: N2O4. This is a molecular formula; reducing it to the empirical ratio NO2 names a different molecular species. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: N₂O₄ must not be reduced to NO₂: that would describe a different molecular species. Ionic formulas use smallest whole-ion ratios; molecular formulas preserve the stated atom counts.

1. Find the pieces: Magnesium is Mg²⁺. Chlorate is the whole polyatomic ion ClO₃⁻; use the ion list if you do not recognize it yet. | 2. Decide the type: Use the ionic route. Two chlorate ions, each −1, balance one Mg²⁺. Copy the whole ClO₃ group twice. | 3. Build the answer: Mg2+ needs two chlorate ions, each ClO3−. Write Mg(ClO3)2 to retain both complete groups. Chlorite is ClO2− and must not be substituted. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: MgClO₃ has only one negative charge. ClO₂⁻ is chlorite, not chlorate. MgClO₆ has one chlorine instead of two and does not preserve two intact chlorate ions.

1. Find the pieces: Silver uses the usual course ion Ag⁺. Cyanide is the whole CN⁻ ion, with carbon and nitrogen together. | 2. Decide the type: Use the ionic route. One +1 silver ion balances one −1 cyanide ion, producing a 1:1 whole-ion ratio. | 3. Build the answer: Ag+ and cyanide, CN−, balance 1:1: AgCN. Keep carbon and nitrogen together; cyanate would include oxygen and is a different ion. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Ag₂CN has net +1 and Ag(CN)₂ has net −1. Adding O changes cyanide into a different ion. A single CN group does not need parentheses.

1. Find the pieces: Boron is a metalloid and fluorine a nonmetal. Boron trifluoride is a known molecular covalent compound, not an ordinary metal–anion salt. | 2. Decide the type: Use the covalent route. No prefix on boron means one B atom; tri- on fluoride means three F atoms. Shared electron pairs form the bonds in this molecular example. | 3. Build the answer: Boron trifluoride is a molecular covalent compound. No first prefix means one boron; tri- gives three fluorine atoms. Write BF3 rather than using ionic charge crossing. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: B₃F puts three on boron instead of fluorine. BF and BF₂ lose the tri- count. The octet rule is not a classification test: boron’s incomplete octet here does not make the compound ionic.

sets.title: Q13 quiz · ionic and covalent naming
sets.description: Work through all 21 original questions. Choose the missing name or formula and the compound type. Start with a hint when needed, then open Ms. Luminara’s full walkthrough. These are practice checks, not a submitted course grade.

rows.explanation: III gives the charge on each iron ion, not a subscript to copy. Oxide is O²⁻; balance total positive and negative charge.
Sulfide is S²⁻. With one sulfide and one nickel, nickel must be +2. Sulfate would contain oxygen.
Read the elements in the printed order. Di- belongs to the two chlorine atoms; one oxygen gives monoxide, not dioxide.
P is phosphorus and Br is bromine. Tri- belongs to bromine; bromate would contain oxygen. There is no first-element mono- prefix.
Ammonium NH₄⁺ supplies the positive ion even though no metal appears. The 2 outside (NH₄) copies every atom in that whole ion.

This quiz uses the molecular prefix-naming model for N₂O₅; pentoxide and pentaoxide are accepted spellings. Solid N₂O₅ can be ionic nitronium nitrate, so this naming category is not a claim about every physical state.
Keep sulfate as SO₄²⁻. Change the number of whole potassium ions, not the four oxygen atoms inside sulfate.
Tri- applies to bromine. No first prefix means one nitrogen atom. The lowercase r is part of the symbol Br.
C₂H₃O₂⁻ is acetate, a complete polyatomic ion. Sodium ethanoate is an equivalent name. Carbonate has a different atom inventory.
Hydroxide is OH⁻, including its hydrogen. One whole hydroxide group balances Na⁺; parentheses are not needed for a single group.
SO₄²⁻ is sulfate; sulfite is SO₃²⁻ and sulfide has no oxygen. The sodium subscript counts ions, not a sodium(II) charge.
Carbonate is the whole CO₃²⁻ ion. Do not change its internal oxygen count when balancing potassium ions.
Recognize two whole ions: ammonium NH₄⁺ and nitrate NO₃⁻. No metal is needed. NH₃ is ammonia; NO₂⁻ is nitrite.
Name the printed empirical formula P₂O₃ for this prefix exercise. Ordinary molecular phosphorus(III) oxide is P₄O₆; do not silently substitute it or treat P₂O₃ as its literal molecular atom count.
Di- counts two sulfur atoms, not two carbons. Both are nonmetals; the prefix gives the printed atom count without crossing ionic charges.
Di- gives two nitrogen atoms and tetr(a)- gives four oxygen atoms. Do not reduce N₂O₄ to NO₂: those are different molecular species.
Two whole ClO₃⁻ ions balance Mg²⁺. Parentheses preserve both complete chlorate groups. ClO₂⁻ is chlorite.
Use the usual course ion Ag⁺ and whole cyanide CN⁻. Cyanate includes oxygen and is a different ion.
Boron is a metalloid, and BF₃ is a molecular covalent example. Tri- belongs to fluorine. Boron’s incomplete octet does not turn this into an ionic salt.
Bromine and fluorine are nonmetals. BrF₃ contains three fluorine atoms; tri- does not belong on bromine.

Diboron hexahydride follows the quiz’s binary-prefix pattern. Diborane and diborane(6) also identify B₂H₆ and are accepted. Its covalent bonding includes bridging hydrogens; a name does not imply six ordinary terminal B–H bonds.

B/C/Ge do not receive a universal monatomic charge from this chart.
The complete separate instructor ion list and molecular spelling conventions still need confirmation.
Acid naming and full orbital configurations are later topics.
